parsed.summary: The Lean theorem asserts that some group G : Type exists that is finitely presented (Mathlib's `Group.IsFinitelyPresented`) and is not sofic, under a bespoke but essentially standard definition of soficity. The paper's Theorem 1.1, as excerpted, says that the specific group L_{F2}(1,2)^× is not sofic. Main caveat: the Lean statement never mentions the Leavitt unit group, and the excerpt does not say that group is finitely presented. So the Lean claim is a different existence statement, not a direct encoding of Theorem 1.1.

glossary.plain: d_Hamm(p,q) = |{y : p(y) ≠ q(y)}| / |Y| for permutations p, q of a finite set Y
A map σ : G → Sym(n) with n > 0 and σ(1) = id
glossary.note: Requiring σ(1) = id is a mild extra condition. It is equivalent up to ε-adjustment because almost-multiplicativity at (1,1) forces σ(1) to be close to id.

glossary.plain: For all g, h ∈ F, d(σ(gh), σ(g)σ(h)) < ε, and for all g ∈ F with g ≠ 1, d(σ(g), id) > 1 − ε
For every finite F ⊆ G and every 0 < ε < 1 there is an (F, ε)-good permutation model
glossary.note: The restriction ε < 1 is harmless because the condition is monotone in ε. The definition applies to all groups, not only countable ones, but finitely presented groups are countable.

lean_claims.plain: There exists a group G (in Type 0) that is finitely presented and is not sofic in the sense of the Sofic class.

paper_claims.plain: The unit group L_{F2}(1,2)^× of the binary Leavitt algebra over F2 is not sofic.

coverage.why: Lean is an existence statement that does not identify the Leavitt unit group, which makes it weaker. It also adds finite presentability, which is not asserted in the excerpt, which makes it stronger in that respect.

flags.explanation: The Lean theorem only asserts the existence of some finitely presented non-sofic group. It does not state that L_{F2}(1,2)^× is non-sofic. Finite presentability of the witness is not stated in the excerpt; whether the paper proves it elsewhere is not in the excerpt. The statement therefore neither directly formalizes Theorem 1.1 nor is clearly implied by the excerpt.
flags.probe_idea: Define the Leavitt algebra R as a quotient of FreeAlgebra (ZMod 2) (Fin 4) by the relations in (1). Then state `¬ SoficGroups.Sofic Rˣ` and separately `Group.IsFinitelyPresented Rˣ`.

flags.explanation: The field map_one (σ(1) = 1) and the field size_pos make Sofic slightly more demanding, so ¬Sofic is formally slightly easier. These conditions are equivalent to the standard definition up to adjusting ε.
flags.probe_idea: Prove that Sofic G is equivalent to the same definition with map_one dropped.
